course.title: Philosophy: Knowledge, Mind and Ethics
course.description: Test arguments row by row, meet Gettier and the sceptic, run a mind as a machine table and weigh lives behind the veil.
course.audience: An adult who has met validity and truth tables, as in Logic and Reasoning, and wants a rigorous university-style introduction to philosophy.

paragraphs: Some questions stay open no matter how many facts you collect. Whether a true belief counts as knowledge is one. Whether it can be right to harm one person to save five is another. Philosophy is the study of questions like these, and people take it up because the answers affect how we weigh evidence and how we treat each other.

The method is argument. A philosopher states a claim, gives reasons for it and lets others test those reasons, so the course begins with that skill: reading an argument, checking whether it holds and answering it fairly. The rest applies the skill to three areas. Knowledge asks what it takes to know something and how evidence should change what we believe. Mind asks what a mind is and what makes you the same person over time. Ethics and politics look at consequences, duties, character and the agreements a society rests on.
Each lesson works through one case or thought experiment, with questions along the way and a short check at the end.
outcomes: You'll be able to set an argument out in standard form and say which premise a speaker left unstated.
You'll be able to test whether a conclusion has to follow from its premises by looking for a counterexample.
You'll be able to explain why a Gettier case, a justified true belief that is true by luck, troubles the definition of knowledge.
You'll be able to say how dualism and physicalism differ and what the Chinese Room is meant to show about minds.
You'll be able to compare what a consequentialist, a Kantian and a virtue ethicist would each say about the same moral choice.
introduction.prerequisites: You should already know what a valid argument is and how to read a truth table, as covered in Logic and Reasoning.

concepts.summary: Apply the justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge and see how Gettier cases separate it from knowing.

concepts.summary: Reconstruct the sceptic's closure argument, test it, and compare the replies of Moore, Dretske and Nozick.

concepts.title: Evidence and credence
concepts.summary: Update a degree of belief with Bayes' theorem, using natural frequencies, base rates and likelihood ratios.

concepts.title: Mind and body
concepts.summary: Assess Descartes' case for dualism, Elisabeth's interaction problem and the physicalist alternatives.

concepts.title: Function and the Chinese Room
concepts.summary: Model a mental state by its causal role, see why one role can have many realisers and weigh Searle's Chinese Room.

concepts.title: What makes you you
concepts.summary: Apply Locke's memory criterion, Reid's transitivity objection and Parfit's fission and teleporter cases.

concepts.title: Counting consequences
concepts.summary: Rank acts by their expected outcomes, and see where summing welfare across people gives troubling verdicts.

concepts.title: Duty, persons and the footbridge
concepts.summary: Apply Kant's universal-law and humanity formulations, and compare the switch and footbridge cases.

concepts.title: Character and the mean
concepts.summary: Locate a virtue between two vices, distinguish the mean relative to us from an arithmetic midpoint, and see how virtue is acquired.

concepts.summary: Compare Hobbes's and Locke's social contracts, then choose principles behind Rawls's veil of ignorance with maximin and averages.

lessons.title: Finding the argument

steps.headline: A claim and the reasons given for it

lead.text: Look again at what Maya said. Her remark makes three separate claims, and they don't all do the same job. “We should eat early” is what she wants her friends to accept. “The film starts at seven” and “the restaurant is a half-hour walk away” are her reasons: facts she offers so that eating early looks like the sensible plan.

Philosophers have names for these two jobs. The claim someone wants you to accept is the conclusion. Each claim offered as a reason for it is a premise. A conclusion together with the premises offered for it is an argument. In everyday speech the word often means a quarrel, but here it means a piece of reasoning, and Maya's is a small one with two premises and one conclusion.

afterFigure.text: The figure sets her remark out as a map, with the premises above and the conclusion below. Her second sentence joins two claims with “and”, and each is a premise in its own right, so that one sentence counts as two.

Premise and conclusion are jobs that a claim does inside one piece of reasoning. “The film starts at seven” is a premise for Maya, but in a talk about cinema listings it could be somebody's conclusion. The sentence alone doesn't tell you which job it has. You have to look at what it is doing in the passage, and the next screens give you ways to do that.

model.passage: We should eat early. The film starts at seven, and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away.

premises.text: The film starts at seven.
The restaurant is a half-hour walk away.

conclusion.text: We should eat early.

model.passage: There will be no tables left: the queue already runs out of the door.

premises.text: The queue already runs out of the door.

conclusion.text: There will be no tables left.

lead.text: Reasons can come in a different order from Maya's. This passage gives its reasons first and its claim last. Count the claims it offers as reasons, remembering that one sentence can hold more than one.

steps.headline: Words that point to a reason or a conclusion

lead.text: Maya gave no signposts, and her friends followed her anyway. Often a speaker does add one. Words such as “because”, “since”, “for” and “after all” point to a reason, so what follows them is a premise. Words such as “so”, “hence” and “thus” point to a conclusion. They are called indicator words, and they are the quickest clue you have.

They also show that the conclusion has no fixed place. A groundsman might say that the match will be called off because the pitch is flooded, or that the pitch is flooded, so the match will be called off. The words and the order change while the two claims and their jobs stay the same. In the figure, choose Passage and press Highlight indicator words to see the signposts in each version.

afterFigure.text: Because position can't settle which claim is the conclusion, and indicator words are sometimes missing or used loosely, it helps to have a second test. Ask what the passage is trying to get you to accept. That claim is the conclusion, and the others are there to back it up. Two short passages come next, so you can try both tests.

model.passage: The match will be called off, because the pitch is flooded.

premises.text: The pitch is flooded.

conclusion.text: The match will be called off.

model.passage: Since the pitch is flooded, the match will be called off.

premises.text: The pitch is flooded.

conclusion.text: The match will be called off.

model.passage: The pitch is flooded, so the match will be called off.

premises.text: The pitch is flooded.

conclusion.text: The match will be called off.

lead.text: Indicator words are small and easy to read past. Look at the sentence below and find the one word that does the pointing.
Use the signpost, and ask what the passage as a whole is trying to get you to accept. Then give the conclusion in your own words.

steps.headline: Writing an argument out line by line

lead.text: Spoken arguments are rarely tidy. A speaker may state the conclusion first, pack two premises into one sentence and add a signpost or two. Before you judge such an argument you want to see it plainly, and there is a conventional way to do that.

Take a remark from a village-hall meeting: “We shouldn't repaint the hall yet. After all, the roof still leaks and new paint would be spoiled.” Drop the signposts, give each premise its own numbered line, draw a line under them and write the conclusion last, marked C. The figure shows the result for the hall and for a second passage, with each spoken clause matched to its line. Use the buttons to switch between them.

afterFigure.text: This layout is called standard form. It leaves the speaker's meaning alone and puts the support in view, so you can ask two separate things: whether each premise is true, and whether the premises, if true, would back the conclusion. A tangled sentence makes it hard to ask either.

It also gives you something to point at. If you disagree about the hall, you can now name the line you reject: the roof may have been mended, or perhaps new paint would survive a few drips. The next question returns to how the conclusion was picked out.

steps.headline: The reason nobody said out loud

lead.text: Maya's remark leaves something out. The film starts at seven and the restaurant is half an hour away, but those facts only point towards eating early if two more things hold: nobody wants to miss the start of the film, and dinner takes a good while. She never said either. She didn't need to, because everyone at the table already took them for granted.

Almost every real argument works this way. People leave out whatever seems too obvious to say, and the argument is shorter and smoother for it. A premise that is needed but not stated is an unstated premise, and an argument with one is called an enthymeme. The name goes back to Aristotle's Rhetoric, where it covers this kind of everyday reasoning.

afterFigure.text: To find a missing premise, ask what else would have to be true for the stated reasons to lead to the conclusion. Add it to the list and the argument is complete, so you can see what it rests on. That is often where its weak spot is. Dev's phone could be off because the battery died, and then the added premise is false and the conclusion loses its support. The next question gives you a case to try.

model.passage: We should eat early. The film starts at seven, and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away.

premises.text: The film starts at seven.
The restaurant is a half-hour walk away.
We want to be in our seats by seven.
Dinner takes a good while.

conclusion.text: We should eat early.

model.passage: Dev's phone is switched off, so he must be asleep.

premises.text: Dev's phone is switched off.
Dev only switches his phone off when he is asleep.

conclusion.text: Dev is asleep.

lead.text: A short argument can lean on a premise nobody says. Ask what link is missing between the reason given and the conclusion, then choose the claim that supplies it.

reveal.text: The unstated premise is the bridge, and supplying it shows where the argument is weak. Many solicitors qualified after a degree in another subject, so the premise is less safe than it looks.

model.passage: Mira is a solicitor, so she has a law degree.

premises.text: Every solicitor has a law degree.
Mira is a solicitor.

conclusion.text: Mira has a law degree.

model.passage: The kettle is switched on at the wall, yet the water is cold after five minutes. So the kettle is broken.

premises.text: If the kettle is switched on at the wall and works, it heats the water.
The kettle is switched on at the wall.
The water is cold after five minutes.

conclusion.text: The kettle does not work.

steps.headline: When one conclusion feeds the next

lead.text: Real reasoning is rarely one step long. Suppose Tom asks Maya how early she means. She could answer: “The film starts at seven and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away, so we must leave the restaurant by half past six. A meal takes about an hour, so we should be sitting down by half past five.”

That is two arguments joined together. The first uses two premises to reach “we must leave the restaurant by half past six”. That claim is a conclusion, but it then serves as a premise in the second step, which adds “a meal takes about an hour” and reaches “we should be sitting down by half past five”. A conclusion that is used again as a premise is an intermediate conclusion. The claim the whole chain is aiming at is the final conclusion. The figure draws the two steps as one chain, and its buttons challenge one claim at a time.

afterFigure.text: Mapping a chain shows where an objection would do the most damage. If Tom shows that the meal takes forty minutes, only the second step is affected. If he shows that the walk takes an hour, the first conclusion changes and the second changes with it. Indicator words help here too: each “so” marks a conclusion, and the last one marks the final conclusion.

blocks.text: Maya and three friends are planning a Friday evening: dinner first, then a film. She glances at the clock and says, “We should eat early. The film starts at seven, and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away.” The others nod and start looking for their coats.

Suppose one of them, Tom, isn't convinced. Saying “no” will get him nowhere, because Maya has given him something to work with. To answer her properly he has to see what she is asking everyone to accept and what she is relying on to get them there. She never labelled either, and she took a few things for granted that she didn't say at all.

People reason like this at work and at home, and most of it goes by without anyone looking closely. Philosophy starts by slowing it down. The first skill in this course is taking a short piece of reasoning like Maya's apart and seeing what each claim is there to do.

recap.keyIdea: An argument is a conclusion backed by premises. Find the conclusion first, then list the premises offered for it and add any premise the speaker took for granted.

lessons.title: Valid, sound and counterexamples

lead.text: Start with Dev's remark and test it. Suppose the rule on the note holds and Ruth did use the last of the milk. Try to describe a situation in which she did not buy more. You will find that you can't, because the rule forbids it. Once the premises are granted, the conclusion cannot be false.

An argument like that is called valid. Validity is about the link between the premises and the conclusion, and you judge it by trying to break the link: looking for a possible situation in which every premise is true and the conclusion is false. Such a situation is a counterexample, and an argument that has one is invalid. The figure sets each remark against a possible situation, and its buttons switch between Dev's remark and Sam's.

afterFigure.text: Now try the same on Sam's. The rule holds and Ruth did bring in a carton, yet it is easy to describe a situation where the conclusion fails: someone else used the last of the office milk, and Ruth bought a carton because her own fridge at home was empty. Both premises are true and the conclusion is false, so the argument is invalid.

One counterexample is enough. You don't have to show that the situation really happened, only that it could, with the premises true and the conclusion false. That is why testing an argument is a search. You are hunting for a single case that breaks it, and you are allowed to make the case up.

steps.headline: Checking every case with a table

lead.text: Hunting for a counterexample by imagination works for small cases, but it depends on your thinking of the right situation. A table makes sure you have looked everywhere. Replace each simple claim in the argument with a letter, then list every combination of true and false for those letters.

Take the pavement again, this time with the second premise changed: “If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet. It rained overnight. So the pavement is wet.” Let p stand for “it rained overnight” and q for “the pavement is wet”. Claims like these, with no smaller sentences inside them, are called atomic sentences. With the letters in place the argument is reduced to its form: p → q, p, so q. The arrow reads “if p then q”, and p → q is false only when p is true and q is false, like a promise that is broken only when the condition holds and the result doesn't follow.

Two atomic sentences can be true or false in four combinations. Write them all out, with the premises and the conclusion worked out for each. That list is called a truth table. Each combination is a row, and a row describes one possible situation.

afterFigure.text: Read the first case. Only one row makes both premises true: p true and q true. The conclusion q is true in that row too, so no row has true premises and a false conclusion. There is no counterexample, and the argument is valid. Step through the second case's rows to see which one breaks it.

premises.text: If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet.
It rained overnight.

conclusion.text: The pavement is wet.

premises.text: If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet.
It did not rain overnight.

conclusion.text: The pavement is not wet.

lead.text: The table settles validity, and the reason has to do with what a counterexample is.

Now the pavement argument you judged earlier, written in letters: p → q, q, so p. List its four rows, by hand or by stepping through them in the figure, and count the ones where both premises are true.

reveal.text: You counted by hand: two rows keep both premises true, and in one of them p is false while q is true. That row is the counterexample, the night when something other than rain wet the pavement.

premises.text: If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet.
The pavement is wet.

conclusion.text: It rained overnight.

premises.text: If the lamp is plugged in, the room is lit.
The room is lit.

conclusion.text: The lamp is plugged in.

lead.text: The table gave the same verdict whatever p and q stand for. Rain and pavements, milk and offices: the letters stand for any of them. That means validity belongs to the pattern of an argument, its form, and a form that passes the table passes for every argument that fits it.

A few forms are common enough to have names. “If p then q; p; so q” is modus ponens, which the table showed to be valid. “If p then q; q; so p” is affirming the consequent, the pattern behind Sam's remark about the milk and the wet pavement, and the table showed it to be invalid. A third valid form is “p or q; not p; so q”, called disjunctive syllogism: if one of two options is ruled out, the other remains.

afterFigure.text: Knowing the names lets you recognise a form on sight, but the table stays in charge. When a form is new to you, build the table or hunt for a counterexample, and don't rely on a name or a feeling that it looks right. Some invalid forms feel very convincing, and the next lesson looks at several of them.

lead.text: Real arguments rarely stop at two atomic sentences. Each extra letter doubles the number of rows, because every existing row splits into one where the new letter is true and one where it is false. Two letters give four rows, three give eight and four give sixteen. By ten letters there are more than a thousand.

That is fine for a short argument and tedious for a long one, so it pays to search with some direction. Start from the conclusion. A conclusion of the form p → r is false only in the rows where p is true and r is false. Fix those two values, then ask what each premise needs from the remaining letter q. If no value of q keeps every premise true, there is no counterexample. If some value does, you have found one.

afterFigure.text: Work it through for the chain in the figure's first case. The conclusion p → r is false only when p is true and r is false, which leaves two rows, one with q true and one with q false. In the first, the second premise q → r fails, since q is true and r is false. In the second, the first premise p → q fails. Neither row keeps both premises true, so the chain is valid. You checked two rows instead of eight. The second case tries the same search on a conclusion that goes the other way.

steps.headline: Valid is not the same as true

lead.text: So far you have asked only whether the conclusion would have to be true if the premises were. You haven't asked whether the premises are true. Compare two arguments. “All mammals breathe air; whales are mammals; so whales breathe air.” “All cats are reptiles; Whiskers is a cat; so Whiskers is a reptile.” Both are valid, because in each case true premises would force the conclusion.

The difference is in the premises. Everything in the first argument is true. The second begins with a falsehood, so its conclusion is false even though nothing is wrong with the reasoning. A valid argument whose premises are all true is called sound. A valid argument with a false premise, like the cats, is unsound, and it gives you no guarantee that its conclusion is true. The figure sets out the four combinations of valid or invalid with true or false premises, then places these examples in it.

afterFigure.text: Soundness is what you want from an argument, and validity is the half that logic can check by itself. The other half is a matter of checking facts. One consequence is worth holding on to: if an argument is valid and its conclusion is false, at least one premise must be false, since true premises would have forced a true conclusion. So when a valid argument has a conclusion you can't accept, look at its premises.

blocks.text: The office kitchen has a note by the fridge: whoever uses the last of the milk buys more. One morning Dev says, “Ruth used the last of the milk yesterday, so she'll have bought some more.” Nobody argues. Later Sam says, “Ruth came in with a carton this afternoon, so she must be the one who used the last of it.” This time people frown, although the two remarks look alike on the page. Each puts the rule beside a fact and draws a conclusion.

Dev's remark leaves no way out. If the rule holds and Ruth used the last of the milk, she bought more, whatever else was going on. Sam's remark leaves a gap, because Ruth could have bought milk for her own kitchen. The two look the same until you test them, and spotting the gap quickly and exactly is a skill.
Last lesson you learned to lay an argument out. This lesson asks how firmly its premises hold up its conclusion, and it gives you a test you can run on any argument, in your head or on paper.

recap.keyIdea: An argument is valid when no possible situation makes every premise true and the conclusion false. It is sound when it is also valid and every premise is true.

lessons.title: Fallacies and charity

steps.headline: Fallacies, starting with attacks on the person

lead.text: The neighbour's remark is an example of a fallacy: a pattern of reasoning that looks convincing and fails. Fallacies are worth learning because they come back. The same few slips turn up in school meetings and in parliament alike, and once you can name one you can spot it each time it returns.

This one has a Latin name, ad hominem, which means “to the person”. It dismisses an argument by pointing at something about the person who makes it, such as her diet or her job. Those facts can matter when you are deciding whether to trust what someone reports. They can't settle whether the reasons she gives are good. Jo's case can be weighed against the price of greens and the health of the children, whatever she eats at home.

afterFigure.text: The figure sets out the neighbour's reply as an argument. To make it work you have to supply an unstated premise, as in the first lesson: that nothing a vegetarian says about school meals deserves attention. Written out, it is plainly too strong to accept. A good test for this slip is to imagine someone else, a meat-eater, making the same suggestion. The reply no longer applies, which shows it was never about the suggestion.

model.passage: Jo's a vegetarian, so ignore her.

premises.text: Jo is a vegetarian.
Nothing a vegetarian says about school meals deserves attention.

conclusion.text: Jo's suggestion can be ignored.

model.passage: Ignore her review of the phone, since she works in the shop.

premises.text: She works in the phone shop.
Nothing a shop worker says about a phone deserves attention.

conclusion.text: Her review of the phone can be ignored.

lead.text: Compare what Dr Okafor argued with what the councillor answered. Then give the pattern its name.

Suppose the meeting returns to Jo's idea and she makes it specific: one meat-free day a week in the canteen. A parent answers, “So Jo wants to stop our children eating meat.” That reply answers a different proposal from the one Jo made. She suggested one day a week, and the parent has answered a ban.

Swapping someone's position for a weaker or more extreme one and then defeating that is called a straw man, after a man made of straw, who is easy to knock over. The reply may even be a good one against the ban. It simply doesn't touch Jo's view, so her proposal is left standing. The figure follows the arrow from the parent's reply, once to the wrong target and once, in the second view, to the right one.

afterFigure.text: The cure is a habit. Before you answer anyone, restate their view in words they would accept, and check that what you are about to attack is that view. The same habit matters again at the end of this lesson.

Some slips hide inside a single word. Here is a small case: “Nothing is better than a day at the beach. A cold, wet Monday is better than nothing. So a cold, wet Monday is better than a day at the beach.” Each premise is acceptable on its own, and the conclusion is plainly wrong.

The trouble is the word “nothing”. In the first premise it means that no activity beats a day at the beach. In the second it means the absence of anything at all. The argument only seems to work because the same word appears twice. Using a word in two senses within one argument is called equivocation. Words with two ordinary meanings, such as “bank” and “fine”, are the usual culprits. The figure shows where the word sits in each premise.

afterFigure.text: The test is to take each key word and check that it means the same thing in every premise. If the meaning shifts, the argument may be valid in appearance only.

steps.headline: Going in circles, and false choices

lead.text: Two more slips concern the support itself. The first is begging the question: a premise that already assumes the conclusion. Take “Parking in the town centre should be free, because it ought not to cost anything to park there.” The reason is the conclusion in other words, so nothing has been added. The circle can be wider and pass through several claims, but it always returns to its starting point.

The second is the false dilemma, which offers two options as if they were the only ones. Back at the meeting someone says, “Either the canteen serves chips every day or the children go hungry.” It sounds forceful because the second option is unthinkable, but the speaker has not shown that there is no third. The question to ask of any either-or is what else is possible. The figure draws each slip in turn.

afterFigure.text: Both slips can be caught by looking at the support. For a circle, trace where the reason comes from and see whether it leads back to the claim. For a dilemma, count the options offered and then count the options that exist.

diagram.alt: Two drawings. In the first, a conclusion about free parking and the reason offered for it say the same thing, so the support loops back to the claim. In the second, an either-or offers two doors, chips every day or hungry children, and leaves out a third door of other options.

Every slip so far makes a reply easier than it should be, and the straw man is the clearest case: it picks the weakest version of a view and calls the job done. The remedy has a name, the principle of charity. Before you criticise an argument, rebuild it in the strongest form its author could reasonably accept, and answer that.

Charity often means supplying a premise, as you did in the first lesson. Return to Jo, who said, “Children aren't eating enough vegetables, so the canteen should serve more.” The step between the two halves is unstated. A weak reading fills it with “Schools should force children to eat vegetables”, which is easy to attack and which Jo never said. A charitable reading fills it with something she would accept, such as “A school canteen should make it easier for children to eat what they are short of”. The figure shows both readings.

afterFigure.text: The charitable reading is the better one to answer, and the reason is practical as well as polite. If you can beat the strongest version, your reply also covers the weaker ones, and if you can't, you have learned something about the argument. You may still reject the argument at the end. If you do, you will have rejected something its author actually holds.

Now use charity on a new argument. Choose the added premise that a thoughtful speaker would accept and that makes the step from reason to conclusion work.

blocks.text: At a parents' meeting, Jo says the school canteen should serve more vegetables. Her neighbour leans over and murmurs, “Jo's a vegetarian, so ignore her.” A few people smile, and the meeting moves on to the car park.

Nothing in the neighbour's reply needs to be false, because Jo may well be a vegetarian. It still goes wrong. It sounds like a reason, with a “so” in the middle, but it says nothing about whether the canteen should serve more vegetables. Last lesson tested whether premises hold up a conclusion. Here the premise doesn't touch the matter at all, and that is only one of several ways in which reasoning can mislead.

This lesson names the commonest of these slips so you can spot them in other people's reasoning and in your own. It ends with the other half of the skill, which is answering someone's argument at its strongest instead of its weakest.

intro.promise: By the end you'll name common slips in reasoning and rebuild an opponent's argument in its strongest form before you reply.

recap.keyIdea: Name the slip, then answer the best version. Replies go wrong by targeting the person, a different view, a shifting word, a circle or a false choice, and charity means rebuilding the argument fairly before you reply.

blocks.text: You started with a neighbour's brush-off at a parents' meeting and followed the meeting through four more slips: a reply aimed at a view nobody held, a word that changed meaning, a circular reason and a forced choice. You ended by rebuilding Jo's argument at its strongest and choosing the fairest premise for a new one.

recap.nextHook: Arguments are not only about logic. The next lesson asks what it takes for a belief to count as knowledge.

lessons.title: Knowledge and Gettier cases

steps.headline: What a lucky guess is missing

lead.text: Tess's friend is onto something. Compare Tess with Kofi, who stood beside her, watched the coin land heads and said “heads”. Both are right and both are sure, yet nobody hesitates to say that Kofi knew. The difference between the two of them shows what knowing asks for.

Start with the claim itself, that the coin landed heads. If it had landed tails, nobody could know that it landed heads. People can think they know something false, but thinking is all they are doing, so whatever is known has to be true. It also has to be believed. Someone who reads a right answer off a card, with no idea whether to trust it, does not believe the answer and so does not know it.

Tess and Kofi meet both of those requirements, which means something else separates them. Kofi has a reason for his claim, because he saw the coin. Tess has no reason at all. So a third requirement is that the belief rests on good reasons, and the next screen puts the three together.

Put the requirements together and you have the traditional view of knowledge, which goes back to Plato. You know something when it is true, you believe it, and your belief is justified, meaning you have good reasons for it. Knowledge, on this view, is justified true belief.

The definition works like a checklist, and each item rules out a kind of case. Truth rules out the person who is confidently wrong. Belief rules out the person who has the facts in front of them and refuses to accept them. A lucky guess fails the third item. The reasons do not have to amount to proof. A forecaster who predicts sun from good evidence is justified even on the day it pours, and the belief fails the first item.

afterFigure.text: The figure lays each case out in the same order, with the person's reasons on the left, what they believe in the middle and what is really so on the right. The three lamps below it show which items hold, and the verdict follows from them. Every case in this lesson uses the same layout.

A checklist this tidy invites a test. If the three items are all there is to knowing, nobody can pass them and still fall short. The next screens apply the checklist and then go looking for such a case.

model.subject: Kofi
model.evidence: He stood beside the coin and watched it land heads.
model.fact: The coin landed heads, and that is what he saw.

model.subject: Tess
model.evidence: Nothing. She called heads for no reason.

lead.text: Use the checklist on a case where the reasoning is careful and the result is wrong.

For centuries the checklist went unchallenged. Then in 1963 an American philosopher, Edmund Gettier, published a paper of just three pages with the title “Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?”, and his answer was no. His examples are short stories, and the first one runs like this.

Smith and Jones have both applied for the same job. The company president tells Smith that Jones will get it, and Smith has just counted ten coins in Jones's pocket. From those two facts Smith reasons carefully to the conclusion that the man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket.

Then the story turns. The president was wrong, and it is Smith who gets the job. Smith also has ten coins in his own pocket, though he has no idea of it. So the conclusion Smith reached, that the man who gets the job has ten coins in his pocket, turns out to be true. Run the story through the checklist before reading on.
Judge truth against what actually happened, not against Smith's evidence. Judge justification by his reasons at the moment he formed the belief.

reveal.text: You counted three. All three conditions hold, yet his evidence was about Jones while the fact that makes his belief true is about himself.

model.subject: Smith
model.belief: The man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket.
model.evidence: The company president told him Jones will get the job; he counted ten coins in Jones's pocket.
model.fact: Smith gets the job, and Smith happens to have ten coins in his own pocket.

model.subject: Kofi
model.evidence: He stood beside the coin and watched it land heads.
model.fact: The coin landed heads, and that is what he saw.

lead.text: So Smith's belief passes every item on the checklist, and still nobody wants to say that he knew it. His reasons were all about Jones. What made his belief true was a fact about Smith himself, and the two never touched. The truth arrived by luck, and the reasons had nothing to do with it.

A case like this is called a Gettier case: a belief that passes the whole checklist but is true only by luck. Gettier's point was that justified true belief cannot be the whole story about knowledge, because the checklist says yes where our judgement says no.

afterFigure.text: The figure sets Smith beside Kofi. When Kofi's reasons and the fact are connected, the match between belief and world is no accident. When they come apart, as Smith's do, the match is luck, no matter how good the reasons looked. That gives a second thing to check beyond the three lamps, which is whether the reasons are tied to what makes the belief true.

model.subject: Smith
model.belief: The man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket.
model.evidence: The company president told him Jones will get the job; he counted ten coins in Jones's pocket.
model.fact: Smith gets the job, and Smith happens to have ten coins in his own pocket.

model.subject: Kofi
model.evidence: He stood beside the coin and watched it land heads.
model.fact: The coin landed heads, and that is what he saw.

steps.headline: Ravi looks out of the window, sees rain falling and believes it is raining. Does he know?

workedSteps.text: True? Yes, it is raining.
Believed and justified? Yes. He believes it, and he can see it.
Here the justification is connected to the fact: the rain is what he sees.
So the checklist says knowledge, and so does intuition.

steps.headline: Ana reads a usually reliable station clock showing 2:15. It is 2:15, but the clock stopped twelve hours ago.

workedSteps.text: True? Yes, it is 2:15.
Believed and justified? Yes. Reading a usually reliable clock is a good reason.
Apply the checklist.

model.subject: Ana
model.evidence: The station clock, usually reliable, reads 2:15.
model.fact: It is 2:15, but the clock stopped exactly twelve hours ago.

model.subject: Ravi
model.evidence: He looks out of the window and sees rain falling on the street.
model.fact: It is raining, and the rain is what he sees.

lead.text: Ana's case leaves the checklist in an awkward place. It says she knows the time, and nearly everyone judges that she does not. Before asking what to do about that, it helps to have two words for how a requirement relates to a result.

A requirement is necessary when the result cannot happen without it. Oxygen is necessary for a fire, because with no oxygen there is no fire. A requirement, or a group of them, is sufficient when having it guarantees the result. Oxygen alone is not sufficient, since a room full of oxygen can sit there without a fire. You also need fuel and heat.

Most philosophers in this debate agree that truth, belief and good reasons are each necessary for knowledge. What a Gettier case tests is the other word, which is whether having all three guarantees knowledge.
Recall what the checklist said about Smith and about Ana, and what we judged about each.

steps.headline: A fourth item for the checklist

lead.text: Gettier's paper set off a long search for a repair, and the simplest idea is to add a fourth item. Look again at Smith. His reasoning began from the claim that Jones will get the job, and that claim was false. Everything he went on to conclude rested on it. Perhaps a belief counts as knowledge only if the reasoning behind it passes through no falsehood.

A step in someone's reasoning is called a lemma, so this fourth item is known as the no false lemmas condition. It also handles Gettier's second case. Smith has always seen Jones drive a Ford and has just been offered a ride in one, so he believes that Jones owns a Ford. From that he infers “Either Jones owns a Ford or Brown is in Barcelona”. He has no idea where Brown is, but a sentence of the form “A or B” is true if only one part is true. Jones in fact rents the car, and Brown happens to be in Barcelona, so the sentence is true by coincidence.

afterFigure.text: Both figures light every lamp, and each has a false belief about Jones early in the reasoning. The fourth item is built to catch exactly that. Some cases have no false step at all, and the next screen looks at those.

model.subject: Smith
model.belief: Either Jones owns a Ford or Brown is in Barcelona.
model.evidence: Jones has always driven a Ford and has just offered Smith a ride in one.
model.fact: Jones rents the car and owns no Ford; by chance, Brown is in Barcelona.

model.subject: Smith
model.belief: The man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket.
model.evidence: The company president told him Jones will get the job; he counted ten coins in Jones's pocket.
model.fact: Smith gets the job, and Smith happens to have ten coins in his own pocket.

lead.text: A different repair looks at how close the belief came to being false. Tess's guess could easily have gone the other way, since heads and tails were equally likely. Kofi, watching the coin, would have said tails had it landed tails. A belief is safe when it would still be true in any nearby situation where you formed it in the same way. Kofi's belief is safe and Tess's is not.

Ana's stopped clock is unsafe as well. Had she come to the station at some other time, she would still have read 2:15 and believed it, and she would have been wrong. This gives a second test, and it works even when no false step appears in the reasoning. Ask what the person would have believed had things been slightly different, and whether that belief would still have been true.

Safety is one of several repairs that philosophers have proposed, and none has won general agreement. It is worth trying on a case that was built to have no false step, and the last practice screen is one of those.
Carl Ginet's fake-barn case, published by Alvin Goldman in 1976, has no false step in the reasoning to blame. Henry sees a real barn in a county full of barn facades.
Ask what Henry would have believed had he glanced at another building.

reveal.text: Henry's belief is not safe: it could easily have been false. Safety explains why he lacks knowledge, whereas no false lemmas, which blames a false belief in the reasoning, does not.

model.subject: Henry
model.evidence: He sees a barn clearly from the road in good light.
model.fact: It is the one real barn in a county full of barn facades.

model.subject: Ana
model.evidence: The station clock, usually reliable, reads 2:15.
model.fact: It is 2:15, but the clock stopped exactly twelve hours ago.

blocks.text: The last lesson showed how reasoning can go wrong. This one asks what a person needs in order to know something. Everyone says “I know” many times a day, and most of the time nobody stops to ask what it takes. A coin makes the question hard to avoid. Tess flips a coin and calls “heads” for no reason at all. It lands heads. Her friend says she didn't really know, she just got lucky.

Most of us agree with the friend, though it is hard to say why. Tess was right, and she was sure. Whatever the friend has noticed, it is something beyond being right and feeling certain, and philosophers have spent a long time trying to say what it is.

This lesson follows the most famous answer, which says that knowledge is a belief with three features. We test that answer on a handful of cases until a three-page paper from 1963 breaks it. After that we look at how people tried to mend it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll test a belief against three conditions for knowledge and explain why a case from 1963 shows they are not enough.

recap.keyIdea: Knowledge needs more than a true belief with good reasons. A Gettier case meets all three conditions and is still true by luck, and repairs such as no false lemmas and safety try to say what is missing.

blocks.text: You started with a lucky guess and built a three-item checklist for knowing. Smith, Ravi and Ana went through the checklist next, and then two repairs were tried on the fake-barn county.

lessons.title: Dreams, demons and closure

lead.text: Descartes began his Meditations of 1641 by asking how much of what he believed he could really rely on. Most of it came through the senses, and the senses sometimes mislead: a stick looks bent in water, and a tower seen from far off looks round. These mistakes are easy to spot afterwards, so they do not seem serious.

Dreams are harder. While you dream you take what you see for real, and nothing in the dream announces that it is one. Descartes sat by his fire in a dressing gown, quite sure he was awake, and still could not name a sign that would separate waking from sleeping with certainty. If he could be asleep at that moment, nothing the senses seemed to show him was guaranteed.

The dream leaves something standing, though. Two and three make five whether you are awake or asleep, and a square has four sides either way. A dream can explain how the senses lead us astray, but arithmetic does not depend on the senses. To reach it, the doubt would have to go further.

So Descartes imagined something stronger than a dream. Suppose that a demon of great cunning and power has set out to deceive him, so that everything he seems to see and hear is an illusion the demon has planted. The same demon could make him go wrong every time he adds two and three.

This is the first example of what philosophers call a sceptical hypothesis: a story on which things seem exactly as they do now but are not as they seem. Nothing in your experience can refute such a story, because the story says your experience is what is being faked. A dream is a mild version. A modern version has you as a brain kept alive in a vat, fed signals by a computer.

Descartes found one thing the demon cannot touch. To be deceived at all, there must be someone who is deceived. Whatever else is false, he exists while he is being fooled, so “I exist” survives the strongest doubt he could devise. That gave him a place to start building, but it left ordinary knowledge of the world, such as knowing that you have hands, exposed.
Compare what a dream could make us doubt with what the demon could.

Modern sceptics do not ask you to believe in a demon. They put the demon to work inside an argument, and the argument starts from an ordinary thought. Say you claim to know that the shop on the corner is open. If you know that, you must also know that it has not burned down overnight, because a burned-down shop is not open. Hardly anyone objects to this step. When you know something and you know that it guarantees something else, you know the other thing too. Philosophers call this principle closure, since what you know stays closed under what you can see it guarantees.

Now apply it to yourself. Having hands rules out being a handless victim of the demon, so closure says that if you know you have hands, you know you are not being deceived. The sceptic then adds a second premise: you cannot know you are not being deceived, because a deception that works feels exactly like no deception.

Logicians shorten this by letting p stand for “I know I have hands” and q for “I know I am not deceived”. Closure supplies the first premise, if p then q, written p → q. The second premise says q is false, written ¬q. The conclusion is that p is false, written ¬p, which means you do not know you have hands. The next screen checks whether that conclusion really follows.
Test the shape as you would any argument: look for a case where both premises hold and the conclusion fails.

reveal.text: You tested the shape. The form p → q, ¬q, so ¬p is called modus tollens, and it has no counterexample row, so the argument is valid. A reply has to reject a premise.

lead.text: Looking for a counterexample by imagination is quick, but a truth table makes the check mechanical. With two letters there are four rows, one for each way that p and q can be true or false. An argument form is valid when no row makes every premise true and the conclusion false, and a row that does is a counterexample.

The conditional p → q is true in both, since a conditional whose first part is false cannot fail. In the row where q is true, the conclusion not q is false. That row has true premises and a false conclusion, so the variant is invalid.

lead.text: A valid argument leaves two choices: accept its conclusion or reject one of its premises. The sceptic's form is modus tollens, from “if p then q” and “not q” to “not p”, and a valid form cannot be answered by finding a fault in the logic. G. E. Moore, a Cambridge philosopher, took the second choice in 1939. In a paper called “Proof of an External World” he held up his hands and said, “Here is one hand.”

Moore kept the first premise and reversed the second. Instead of “I do not know I am not deceived” he began from “I know I have hands”. From p → q and p, the conclusion q follows by modus ponens, the mirror image of modus tollens: from “if p then q” and p, infer q. It is valid for the same reason as the sceptic's argument, since no row makes the premises true and the conclusion false.

So there are two valid arguments that share their first premise and end in opposite conclusions. Validity cannot settle the dispute, because both arguments have it. The question becomes which second premise deserves more trust, the sceptic's “I do not know I am not deceived” or Moore's “I know I have hands”. Moore said he was more certain of his hands than of any philosophical premise that could be set against them.

lead.text: Moore kept closure and denied the sceptic's second premise. There is another way out, which goes after the first premise instead. Fred Dretske and Robert Nozick, writing in the 1970s and 1980s, started from what it takes to know something. To know that you have hands, they said, your belief must be tied to the facts: if you did not have hands, you would not believe that you did. For ordinary people that tie holds.

Now take the claim that you are not a handless brain in a vat. If you were such a brain, you would still believe that you were not, because the vat feeds you the same experiences as before. Your belief is not tied to the fact in the same way, so Dretske and Nozick say that you cannot know it.

They accept the sceptic's second premise and they say that you know you have hands. Those two verdicts clash with the sceptic's first premise, and they accept that clash. In their view you can know one thing without knowing something it guarantees. The price is that this sounds odd: you know you have hands, yet you do not know you are not a handless brain in a vat.
Dretske and Nozick accept that you know you have hands. They deny that you can know you are not a handless brain in a vat.
Ask which general principle about knowledge those two verdicts contradict.

reveal.text: That principle is closure: if you know p, and know that p entails q, you know q. The sceptic's first premise is an instance of it, and Dretske and Nozick pay for their reply by giving it up.

That ordinary experience is the seed of one of philosophy's oldest worries. If a dream can feel exactly like waking life, no feeling can prove to you that you are awake. lessons.title: Evidence and credence

lead.text: A phrase such as “the test is 90% accurate” hides most of what you need, and the way to see what a result means is to count people. Take a town of 1,000 people in which 200 have a condition, and run one test on everyone. The test can go wrong in two directions.

It can miss people who have the condition, and it can flag people who do not. The share of ill people it flags is called the hit rate. The share of healthy people it flags is called the false alarm rate. Say the hit rate is 60% and the false alarm rate is 5%. Among the 200 ill people the test flags 120. Among the 800 healthy people it flags 40.

afterFigure.text: That makes 160 flagged people in all, and they come from two groups. Anyone who reads a flag as “this person is ill” has forgotten the 40 healthy people in the crowd. The second case shows what a lower false alarm rate does to the crowd. The next screens turn the count into a measure of how far a flag should change your mind.

lead.text: The test flags people in two groups, the ill and the well. Count both.

Before anyone is tested, the chance that a person picked from the town has the condition is 200 in 1,000, or 20%. That starting figure is called the prior: how likely a hypothesis was before the new evidence arrived.

Now someone is flagged. Of the 160 flagged people, 120 are ill. That is 120 out of 160, or 75%. That figure is the posterior: how likely the hypothesis is once the evidence is in. The flag has moved the chance of illness from a prior of 20% to a posterior of 75%.

Notice which count was divided by which. The posterior is a share of the flagged people, so the total at the bottom has to include everyone who was flagged, ill or not. The prior is a share of the whole town, which answers a different question. Dividing the ill positives by all the positives is the method this lesson keeps returning to.
The prior comes before the evidence, and the test is part of the evidence. Decide which quantity is which.
Picture the 1,000 people in two groups, the ill and the well. The test flags people in both.
Of everyone who is flagged, ask how many are ill.

reveal.text: You counted the positives from both groups. A positive result leaves a 50% chance of illness, far below the test's 90% hit rate.

steps.headline: A test catches 80% of cases and flags 5% of healthy people. 20% of 1,000 people have the condition. What share of positives are ill?

workedSteps.text: Split the 1,000 people.
Count the positives in each group.
Divide the ill positives by all positives.

lead.text: Run a test with a 90% hit rate and a 5% false alarm rate in a town where the condition is rare. Of 1,000 people, 20 are ill and the test flags 18 of them. The other 980 people are healthy, and 5% of them is 49 false alarms. That makes 67 flagged people, and only 18 of them, about 27%, are ill.

The hit rate is as good as before, yet a flag now leaves you more likely to be healthy than ill. The reason is the size of the two groups. A small error rate applied to a very large healthy group produces more false alarms than a high hit rate applied to a handful of ill people produces hits. How common the condition was before testing is called the base rate, and it decides how much weight a flag deserves.

Judging a result by the hit rate alone and forgetting the base rate is a common mistake, called base-rate neglect. It is the thought that a positive result from a 90% test means you are 90% likely to be ill.

steps.headline: The same 90% hit rate and 10% false alarms, now on a condition that affects 1% of 1,000 people.

reveal.text: A positive result now means illness only 9 times in 108, about 8%. Judging a test by its hit rate while ignoring how rare the condition is, is called base-rate neglect.

workedSteps.text: Find how many people are ill, and how many of them the test catches.
Apply the false-alarm rate to everyone who is well, and add the two groups of positives.

lead.text: There is a shortcut for the counting. Odds compare the ill with the healthy instead of with everyone: 200 ill people and 800 healthy ones are odds of 1 to 4. These are the odds before the test, so they are called the prior odds.

A flag changes the odds by a fixed factor. The factor is the hit rate divided by the false alarm rate, so here it is 60% ÷ 5% = 12. It is called the likelihood ratio: how many times more likely a flag is for an ill person than for a healthy one. Multiply the prior odds by it and you get the posterior odds. Odds of 1 to 4 become 12 to 4, which is 3 to 1.

Odds of 3 to 1 mean three ill people for every healthy one among the flagged, which is 75% and agrees with the count of 120 and 40. The same test multiplies the odds by the same factor wherever it is used. That is why the base rate matters: a factor of 12 applied to small prior odds still gives small posterior odds.
The same shortcut works for any test. Work out the factor for the test in the question, then compare the three towns in the figure.

reveal.text: A 10% prior is odds of 1 to 9. Multiplying by the ratio gives even odds, which is 50%. A 1% prior is 1 to 99, and the same test lifts it only to 9 to 99.

lead.text: Textbooks write all of this in symbols. Let H stand for the hypothesis “this person is ill” and E for the evidence “the test is positive”. The prior is written P(H), the probability of H. The hit rate is P(E | H), which reads as the probability of E given H. The false alarm rate is P(E | not-H).

The posterior is P(H | E). Counting gives it as the ill positives over all positives. In the first town, P(H) = 0.2, P(E | H) = 0.6 and P(E | not-H) = 0.05. The ill positives make up 0.2 × 0.6 = 0.12 of the town, and the healthy positives make up 0.8 × 0.05 = 0.04 of it. So P(H | E) = 0.12 ÷ (0.12 + 0.04) = 0.75.

Written in full this is Bayes' theorem: P(H | E) = P(E | H) × P(H) ÷ P(E), where P(E) is the share of the whole town that tests positive. Each symbol is something you have already counted. When a question gives probabilities, turn them into a town of people and the answer is a division of two counts.
Change one number at a time and recount. Here the test is weaker at catching cases but gives fewer false alarms, and the condition affects one person in ten.

reveal.text: Lowering false alarms usually does more for a rare condition than raising the hit rate, because most positives then come from the healthy group.

blocks.text: Most real doubt comes in degrees, and a medical test is a good place to see it. A clinic tells you that a test for a condition catches nine in ten of the people who have it. Yours has come back positive. Your first thought is probably that you are 90% likely to have the condition, and that thought can be wrong by a wide margin. The test itself may be sound. What the 90% leaves out is how common the condition was to begin with.

The way to see this is to stop thinking in percentages and count people. Imagine a town of 1,000 people in which 100 have the condition, and test all of them. The test flags nine in ten of the ill people. It also flags one in ten of the healthy ones, and there are 900 of those.

lessons.title: Mind and body

lead.text: In the comics, Clark Kent and Superman are one man with two names, though Lois Lane does not know it. She works beside the mild reporter every day and admires the hero who flies past her window. Because there is only one man, anything true of Superman is true of Clark Kent. If Superman can fly, so can Clark Kent.

That is a general rule about identity, known as Leibniz's law after the seventeenth-century philosopher Gottfried Leibniz: if A and B are the same thing, then whatever is true of A is true of B. The rule runs in one direction only. It says what must follow from being one thing, and it does not say the reverse.

The rule is most useful for showing that two things are different. If you can find a property that A has and B lacks, then A and B cannot be one thing. A house with a red door cannot be the same house as one without a red door. Descartes uses the rule in exactly this way when he argues that he is not his own body.
Apply the rule to the two names.

In the Meditations Descartes doubted everything he could, and he noticed an asymmetry. He could doubt that his body exists, since a demon or a dream might have invented it. He could not doubt that he himself exists, since doubting is a kind of thinking and something has to be doing the thinking.

He turned this into an argument. His body is something he can doubt exists, and he is not something he can doubt exists. By Leibniz's law, if he were his body then whatever is true of one would be true of the other, so he is not his body. He concluded that a person is a mind, a thinking thing with no size or place, joined to a body that has both. The view that mind and body are two different kinds of thing is called substance dualism, where a substance is something that exists in its own right.

lead.text: If a person is a mind joined to a body, the two must affect each other. A pinprick in a finger produces a feeling of pain, and a decision to raise your arm produces a raised arm. In 1643 Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia wrote to Descartes to ask how this could work.

Descartes held that bodies are extended, which means they take up space, while minds are not. A billiard ball moves another by touching it and pushing. Elisabeth asked how something with no size or place could touch anything, let alone push a body. If it cannot touch, it seems it cannot move. This objection, how two substances with nothing in common could act on each other, is called the interaction problem.

Descartes replied that we all know from experience that the mind moves the body. He compared the mind's action to heaviness, which pulls a stone down without any contact we can feel. Elisabeth was not persuaded, and she pressed him in further letters. Dualists have been looking for a better answer ever since.
Ask what kind of problem arises when two substances are supposed to act on each other.

Elisabeth's challenge can be written as an argument and tested as the sceptic's was in the last lesson. Let p stand for “the mind moves the body”, q for “the mind touches the body” and r for “the mind is extended”. Her first premise says that if the mind moves the body, it touches it. Her second says that if the mind touches the body, it is extended. Descartes accepts the third, that the mind is not extended.

In symbols the premises are p → q, q → r and ¬r, and the conclusion is ¬p, that the mind does not move the body. With three letters there are eight rows. To test the argument, start from ¬r, which is true only in the rows where r is false, and then see which of those rows keep the other two premises true. The practice question asks how many do.

The result matters for a dualist. If the argument is valid, then anyone who wants to keep the interaction has to deny one of its premises. One choice is to deny the first, that moving something requires touching it. That leaves the dualist to explain a kind of causing that needs no contact.

lead.text: A different response to the interaction problem is to deny that there are two substances. Physicalism holds that everything, minds included, is physical. One argument for it concerns causes. Every physical event that has a cause already has a sufficient physical cause, so if mental events also caused physical ones, each of those events would have two causes. That looks like an odd coincidence, and the simpler view is that the mental events doing the causing are themselves physical.

Physicalists then differ about how a mental state is physical. One view says that each type of mental state just is a type of brain state, in the way that lightning just is electrical discharge. Pain would be a pattern of nerve cells firing and nothing over and above it. This is the identity theory.

A weaker position keeps one physical substance but not a physical account of the mind. Property dualism says there is only one kind of substance, the physical, while mental properties such as the feel of pain are not physical properties. A brain would have both kinds. This avoids two substances, though it still owes an account of how a mental property makes a difference in the physical world.

premises.text: Every physical event that has a cause has a sufficient physical cause.
Some mental events cause physical events.
Those physical events are not caused twice over.

conclusion.text: Those mental events are physical events.

premises.text: If the mind moves the body, it touches the body.
If the mind touches the body, it is extended.
The mind is not extended.

When you picture yourself thinking, you might picture a brain at work, or you might picture something that could never be weighed or photographed, a mind that merely uses the brain. People have argued for both answers for a very long time, and Descartes' answer, that the mind is a separate thing from the body, is still where the debate starts.

His case rests on an argument about what he could doubt, and judging it takes a logical tool that is easiest to meet in a comic book. We start with that tool, use it to test his argument, and then follow the objection that a princess put to him in 1643, which has never been answered to everyone's satisfaction.

lessons.title: Function and the Chinese Room

lead.text: Picture two calculators on a desk. One is built from gears and levers and the other from silicon chips. Press 3 + 4 on each and both show 7. Inside they have nothing in common, and nobody hesitates to say that both are adding.

That shows something about the word. What makes a device an adder is what it does with the numbers it is given: the same inputs go in and the same sums come out. The material makes no difference. Plenty of everyday things are named this way. A thermostat is anything that switches the heating on when it gets cold, whether it is made from a metal strip or a chip, and a cashier is whoever takes the money at the till.

Philosophers call a thing's job in a system its function. An adder's function is to produce sums, and anything that performs that function counts as an adder. The question for this lesson is whether the same could be true of minds. To make the idea exact we first need a simple machine to study.
Think about what makes something an adder.

steps.headline: A drinks machine as a table

lead.text: The philosopher Ned Block used a drinks machine as his example. It sells a can for 20p and takes 10p and 20p coins. It starts with nothing owed. Everything it does can be written as a table, called a machine table. The table lists the states the machine can be in, here “nothing owed” and “10p credited”. For each state and each coin it says what the machine does next, which means the state it moves to and what comes out.

The rules are short. From nothing owed, a 10p moves the machine to 10p credited and nothing comes out. From 10p credited, a 10p completes 20p, so a can comes out and the machine goes back to nothing owed. A 20p from nothing owed buys a can at once. A 20p from 10p credited buys a can and returns 10p.

Notice what the table leaves out. It says nothing about gears, chips or springs. The state “10p credited” is whatever state of the machine turns a further 10p into a can, so a state is identified by its role in the table. Philosophers call this a functional state: a state defined by what it does with inputs and which state it leads to, whatever it is made of.
Use the table to decide what the state called “10p credited” amounts to.
Block's machine sells a can for 20p and starts with nothing owed. Follow the state after each coin, using the rules you have just read.

reveal.text: You ran the table: credit, can, credit again. The state “10p credited” is just whatever role it plays in the next move.

steps.headline: Run the machine on 10p, 20p, 10p from nothing owed. What has come out, and where does it end?

workedSteps.text: 10p from nothing owed: the machine moves to 10p credited. Nothing comes out.
20p with 10p credited: it pays for a can and returns 10p. The machine goes back to nothing owed.
10p again: it moves to 10p credited. In all, one can and 10p change have come out.

steps.headline: Start with nothing owed and insert 20p, then 10p, then 20p.

workedSteps.text: 20p with nothing owed buys a can at once.
10p sets up a credit.
Count the cans after the last coin.

steps.headline: The same table in different materials

lead.text: Now carry the idea over to minds. Functionalism is the view that a mental state is defined by its role in the system. Pain, on this view, is whatever state is caused by injury and in turn produces a wish for it to stop and a tendency to wince and withdraw.

That puts functionalism in competition with the identity theory of the last lesson, which said that pain is one particular brain state. Putnam objected in 1967 that pain seems to occur in humans and in octopuses, whose nervous systems are very different. It might one day occur in silicon too. If pain were one particular brain state, creatures without that state could not feel it. If pain is a role, anything that plays the role can feel it.

afterFigure.text: This is multiple realisability: the same table can be implemented by gears, neurons or chips, so one mental kind can have many different physical realisers. The drinks machine shows the pattern in small, and Putnam's claim is that minds show it too.

lead.text: Putnam used pain in humans, in octopuses and in possible robots as his examples. Name the thesis they support.

If functionalism is right, a machine that plays the right role has a mind. In 1980 John Searle set out to show that this cannot be so. Imagine him locked in a room with a slot in the wall. Slips of paper covered in Chinese characters arrive through the slot. Searle knows no Chinese, and to him the characters are meaningless squiggles. He has a rulebook in English that tells him which characters to pass back out for each batch that comes in.

To the people outside, the room holds a fluent Chinese speaker. They post questions and get sensible answers. Yet Searle understands nothing. He is following rules that connect shapes with shapes, and he has no idea what any of it means. The rulebook plays the part of a machine table, and Searle plays the part of the machine running it.

Searle concludes that running the right program cannot be enough for understanding. A program works on the shapes of symbols, which is syntax, while understanding needs meaning, which is semantics. His slogan is that syntax is not sufficient for semantics. He grants that the room behaves like a speaker of Chinese. What he denies is that behaving like one, by running a program, amounts to understanding.

Searle's argument drew many replies, and the best known is the systems reply. It agrees that the man understands no Chinese and says that this does not matter. The man is one part of a larger system that also contains the rulebook and the slips of paper, and the whole system is what understands. A single neuron in your brain understands no English either.

Searle answered that the man could memorise the whole rulebook and do the work in his head, so that the system would be inside him. He would still understand no Chinese. His critics reply that the memorised system might understand even though the man's ordinary self does not know it, and the two sides have not agreed.

So the disagreement turns on whether playing the right role is enough for a mind. Functionalism says yes. Searle says that the room shows otherwise. Neither side can point to a settled case, which is why the room is still discussed.
Some philosophers agree that the man in the room understands no Chinese, and still say that something in the room understands. Name their reply.

reveal.text: The systems reply says the whole room understands. Searle answers that he could memorise the rules and still understand nothing. His slogan: syntax is not sufficient for semantics.

blocks.text: In a film, an android grips its arm and says that it is in pain. It flinches from the fire, keeps away from it afterwards and describes the pain as you would. Most viewers feel pulled two ways. The android behaves like something in pain, and it is made of metal and wire.

The last lesson ended with physicalists, who say the mind is physical. Some of them add that what matters about a mind is what it does, and what it is made of is beside the point. If they are right, a machine could in principle have a mind. If they are wrong, no machine could, whatever its behaviour.

This lesson starts with a drinks machine, which has no mind but shows plainly what it means to be defined by what something does. It then moves to the claim about minds, and ends in a locked room where a man answers questions in Chinese without understanding a word.

lessons.title: What makes you you

lead.text: The question has a precise meaning, so it helps to pin it down first. When we say the child in the photograph is the same person as you, we do not mean that the two resemble each other, as twins do. We mean that there is one person, who was a child and is now an adult. Philosophers call this question personal identity: what it takes for a person at one time to be one and the same person as a person at another.

An answer is called a criterion of identity, a test that settles for any two people at different times whether they are one person. The first test most of us reach for is the body. On this view you are the person who has the same living body, continuing without a break from the child in the photograph to you. Call it the bodily criterion. It handles the photograph easily, since the child's body grew into yours.
Yet people have long suspected that the body is not the whole story. John Locke argued that what matters is what goes on inside a person's head, and his answer is the next stop.

Locke asked what makes you aware of yourself as the same person through time, and his answer was memory. You are the same person as an earlier part of your life when you can remember its experiences from the inside, as your own. You remember the dive you took last summer in that way, which is quite unlike knowing that it happened because someone told you. Philosophers call each such part of a life a stage.

Put as a test, it reads like this. A later stage is the same person as an earlier stage just when the later one remembers the earlier one's experiences from the inside. Call this the memory criterion. Bodies and names do not enter into it. If your body were swapped for another and your memories went with you, Locke would say that you had gone with the memories.
Notice how direct the test is. It looks only at what a stage itself remembers. Hold on to that, because the next story depends on it.
Use Locke's test on a simple case. Anna is sixty now, and she was twenty once.

Thomas Reid, one of Locke's critics, answered him with a story. A boy is flogged at school for robbing an orchard. Years later, as a young officer, he captures an enemy standard (a military flag) in battle, and he can still remember the flogging. Many years after that he is a retired general. He remembers capturing the standard, but the flogging has slipped completely out of his memory.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows what each stage remembers. One more fact about identity belongs here. If Ann is the same person as Bea, and Bea is the same person as Cy, then Ann is the same person as Cy. Three names, one person, and there is no way for the first and third to differ. Whatever test we adopt for being the same person has to behave this way.
That is all you need for the next question. Take the memory criterion exactly as Locke put it, apply it to the general and to each of his two earlier selves in turn, and see where it leads.

cases.label: The same three stages, by body

lead.text: Apply Locke's test to the old general and each of his two earlier selves, the boy and the officer, one at a time.

reveal.text: You tested the general against each stage separately. He passes for the officer and fails for the boy, though the officer passes for the boy.

steps.headline: Show that the direct memory criterion contradicts itself in Reid's case.

workedSteps.text: The general remembers the officer's deed, so the criterion says the general is the officer.
The officer remembers the flogging, so the criterion says the officer is the boy.
Identity passes along a chain: if the general is the officer and the officer is the boy, the general is the boy. But he remembers nothing of the flogging, so the criterion says he is not.

lead.text: The worked example ended in a clash. Taken stage by stage, the criterion makes the general the officer and the officer the boy, and the same criterion says the general is not the boy. Logicians call the rule it broke transitivity: when a relation holds between a and b and between b and c, it holds between a and c. Identity is transitive, as the Ann, Bea and Cy example showed, so a test that is not transitive cannot be a test of identity.

The usual repair keeps Locke's idea and changes what counts. Look at the whole life and not at single pairs. Memory links the boy to the officer, and it links the officer to the general. Those overlapping links form a chain. On the continuity view, you are the same person as any earlier stage that a chain of this kind joins to yours, even if you cannot remember that stage directly. Because memory and character are both mental, this is also called a psychological criterion.

afterFigure.text: In Reid's case the chain runs from the boy through the officer to the general. On the continuity view all three are one person, which is the verdict Reid's story seems to ask for.

steps.headline: Four stages: A aged 10, B aged 30, C aged 50 and D aged 80. Each remembers only the stage before it.

workedSteps.text: A and B are linked by memory. B and C are linked. C and D are linked. No stage remembers any stage but the one before it.
On the continuity view, count every later stage the chain reaches from A.

lead.text: The continuity view works well for ordinary lives and runs into trouble when they are replaced by imagined ones. Some patients keep much of their memory and character after surgery that removes half of the brain. So suppose a surgeon could split your brain and put each half into a new body, with each half carrying all your memories and your character. Call this fission, the splitting of one person into two.

Two people now wake up. Each remembers your life from the inside, and each has your character. Psychological continuity does not care which body carries the memories. The two are not the same person as each other, since from now on they live separate lives.

afterFigure.text: A criterion that says the same person is whoever is continuous with you would here give two answers, and identity allows only one. Some supporters of the view add a clause that continuity gives identity only when it does not branch. Derek Parfit drew a stronger lesson. He argued that being the very same person was never what mattered. What matters is psychological continuity, which fission leaves in place twice over.

lead.text: Take the continuity view as it stands, with no extra clause, and apply it to the surgery you have just read about.

reveal.text: Two people satisfy the criterion, and they are not one another, so they cannot both be you. That is why the extra clause, or Parfit's lesson, is needed.

lead.text: The same tension shows up with a machine from science fiction. A scanner records the position of every cell in your body and then destroys the body. The record goes to Mars, where another machine builds an exact replica from fresh matter. The replica wakes up remembering your life and with your character, and walks out of the booth.

The two criteria you have met are ready for this case. The bodily criterion follows the living body from one moment to the next. The psychological criterion follows memory and character. In daily life the two agree, because a person's body and mind travel together. The teleporter pulls them apart, which is why philosophers like it.

afterFigure.text: Parfit added a twist, the branch line. Suppose the scanner copies you to Mars but fails to destroy the body on Earth. Now a person on Earth has your body, and a replica on Mars has your memories and character, and each of them remembers your life. Whatever a criterion says about you, it must now say about two people at once.

lead.text: Apply the bodily criterion to the first teleporter, the one that destroys your body on Earth before the replica wakes on Mars.

reveal.text: No body continues to Mars, so on the bodily criterion the replica is a new person. A psychological criterion says you travelled.
