blocks.text: Find the oldest photograph of yourself that you can. The child in it has a different face, a different height, and tastes and fears that you would hardly recognise. Many of the cells that made up that child have been replaced since. You may remember nothing at all of the day the picture was taken.

Even so, you say without a second thought that the child in the picture is you. Nobody has to prove it to you. Something has held you together across all those years, and it is surprisingly hard to say what.

This lesson goes looking for that something. It tries two answers in turn and finds a story that breaks the first. It ends with two cases from science fiction, a brain split in two and a machine that copies a person, where the best answers we have begin to disagree.

intro.promise: By the end you'll test two answers to what makes you the same person, and see where each one breaks.

recap.keyIdea: The direct memory criterion breaks the transitivity of identity, so the continuity view counts chains of memory. Fission and teleporters then pull psychological and bodily criteria apart.

blocks.text: You applied Locke's test to Reid's general and watched it contradict itself. You then counted a chain of memory from age 10 to 80, and followed a split brain and a scanner.

lessons.title: Counting consequences

lead.text: Take a different game from the one you were just offered. A spinner pays £30 when it stops on the blue third of the dial, and nothing when it stops anywhere else. Over 300 plays it should land on blue about a hundred times, which pays about £3,000 in all. Shared across the 300 plays, that is £10 a play. You reach the same figure faster by taking one third of £30.

That shortcut is the whole idea. Multiply what each outcome is worth by the chance that it happens, and add the results. When the outcomes are about how well people's lives go, we measure them in units of welfare, a number for how good or bad an outcome is for those affected. The weighted total is the act's expected utility, the value you would average per play if you could repeat the choice many times.

This matters for ethics because of what consequentialists say. Consequentialism is the view that an act is right or wrong according to its outcomes. Outcomes are often uncertain, so a consequentialist ranks acts by their expected utility and favours the highest. The rest of the lesson tests that rule.
Back to the coin game from the start. Heads pays £100 and tails pays nothing, and you can play again and again.

Expected utility earns its keep when you have to choose. Work out the expected utility of each option and take the larger. Here are two programmes. Programme A almost always gives a modest gain: a 90% chance of 60 units of welfare and a 10% chance of 20. Programme B is bolder: a 50% chance of 120 units and a 50% chance of nothing.

afterFigure.text: A comes to 0.9 × 60 + 0.1 × 20 = 56 units. B comes to 0.5 × 120 + 0.5 × 0 = 60 units. So the rule picks B, even though B fails half the time and A almost never does. Someone cautious might still choose A, since they do not want to risk coming away with nothing. The rule itself reports only the average, and a consequentialist who follows it takes the higher one.

lead.text: Compare a sure thing with a gamble. Work out the gamble's expected utility, then see whether it beats the sure 50 units.

reveal.text: You weighed the gamble: 0.6 × 100 + 0.4 × 0 comes to more than the sure 50. An expected-utility maximiser takes the gamble, and a cautious agent might not.

lead.text: So far every outcome has been a gain. Real choices often carry a risk of harm, and the rule handles that by giving a harm a negative value. A harm of 10 units is entered as −10, and it pulls the total down in proportion to its probability.

Consider a clinic deciding whether to offer a new drug. There is a 50% chance that it helps, by 30 units, and a 50% chance that it harms, by 10 units. Weighting each outcome gives 0.5 × 30 = 15 and 0.5 × (−10) = −5. The total is 10 units. Doing nothing is the baseline and scores 0, so on this rule the clinic should offer the drug.

Notice what the rule compares. It never asks whether the drug is good in itself, only whether its expected utility beats the alternatives on the table. The next screen works through a case one step at a time, and the one after leaves a step for you.

steps.headline: A treatment gives 10 units of benefit with probability 0.7 and causes 20 units of harm with probability 0.3. Is it worth giving?

workedSteps.text: Give the harm a negative value.
Weight each outcome by its probability.
Add them. The total is positive, so the treatment beats doing nothing, which scores 0.

steps.headline: A vaccination programme gives 20 units of benefit with probability 0.9 and causes 30 units of harm with probability 0.1. Should it run?

workedSteps.text: Weight the benefit: probability 0.9 times 20 units.
Weight the harm as a negative: probability 0.1 times −30 units.
Add the weighted values.

lead.text: All these units of welfare stand for something, and a consequentialist has to say what. The most influential answer is utilitarianism, developed by Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill. It says that the right act is the one that does the most good for the most people, and that what counts as good is happiness, meaning pleasure and the absence of pain. Mill put it this way: acts are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness. He called this the greatest happiness principle.

Bentham treated all pleasures alike and counted them by amount, such as how intense they are and how long they last. Mill thought that left something out. Reading poetry and eating sweets can feel equally pleasant and still differ in worth, he said, because some pleasures are higher than others. His own line was that it is 'better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied'. Someone who had known both kinds, he argued, would not give up the higher one for any amount of the lower.
Once happiness is the thing to be measured, it can be added up across a whole community. That step is where the trouble begins.

The principle becomes sharp when lives are at stake. In 1967 the philosopher Philippa Foot described a case now known as the trolley problem. A runaway trolley is heading down the main track towards five people who cannot get out of the way. You are standing next to a lever. If you pull it, the trolley turns onto a side track, where it will kill one person instead.

afterFigure.text: A utilitarian treats this as a sum of lives. If you do nothing, five die, and if you pull the lever, one dies. The difference between those two totals shows what the lever changes, and the utilitarian says to choose the option that leaves the most people alive. Most people, asked about this case, agree that pulling the lever is permitted, so here the theory and common opinion line up. Keep that in mind, because the next lesson shows a case where they part.

cases.label: Five ahead, one on the side
Three ahead, one on the side

lead.text: Count only lives, as a utilitarian does. Compare the two options at the lever.

reveal.text: Pulling the lever saves four lives net: five die if you do nothing and one if you pull.

lead.text: The counting rule has a feature that matters more as the numbers grow. It adds welfare across everyone affected, so many small losses can add up to more than one large harm. Philosophers call this aggregation. Suppose a policy gives two people 3 units each and takes 4 units from a third. The total is 6 − 4 = 2, a net gain, even though one person is worse off.

T. M. Scanlon pushed the idea to an extreme. Jones is trapped in a transmitter room and is receiving painful electric shocks. Freeing him means cutting the broadcast of a match that millions are watching, and the repair takes an hour. Each viewer loses a little enjoyment, but there are millions of them.

afterFigure.text: Added up, the viewers' small losses can outweigh Jones's suffering, so a utilitarian who aggregates may leave him where he is. Critics say this ignores the separateness of persons. The viewers' disappointments are never felt by anyone as one great loss, whereas Jones feels his pain alone.

lead.text: Scanlon's case gives a verdict that many people reject. Look at how the theory reaches it, and name the feature responsible.

reveal.text: That feature is aggregation, summing welfare across people, which lets many small losses outweigh one great harm.

lessons.orientation: Rank acts by their expected outcomes, and see where summing welfare across people gives troubling verdicts.

blocks.text: A friend offers you a game. Flip a coin: heads pays £100 and tails pays nothing. You can play as often as you like, and it costs nothing to play. After one flip you hold either £100 or nothing, so a single play tells you very little about the game. Play it a thousand times and a steady picture appears.

Choices outside games work the same way. A doctor deciding whether to give a treatment cannot know whether it will help this patient, but she knows how often it helps patients like this one. A government deciding whether to run a vaccination programme knows the chances and the stakes. Some philosophers say that every act should be judged like this, by the results it can be expected to bring about.

This lesson starts with the coin and learns to weigh chances against stakes. It then applies the same weighing to a runaway trolley, and ends at a case where the method gives a verdict that many people find hard to accept.

recap.keyIdea: A consequentialist ranks acts by expected utility, weighting every outcome by its probability, with harms as negatives. Adding welfare across people can then outvote one person's great harm.

lessons.title: Duty, persons and the footbridge

steps.headline: What the plan needs from the victim

lead.text: To find what separates the two cases, look at each plan as a piece of machinery. In Case A the plan is to turn the trolley away from the five. It happens that the side track has one person on it, and he is killed. But suppose the side track were empty. The plan would still work and the trolley would still be turned. The death of the one is a foreseen result of the plan, and the plan does not rely on it.
Case B is different. The plan is to stop the trolley with the stranger's body. Take the stranger away and nothing stops the trolley, so the plan fails. His body is a working part of the plan.

afterFigure.text: Philosophers have names for these two roles. When a harm to someone is how your plan works, you are using that person as a means. When a harm is a result that the plan merely brings along, and the plan would work just as well without it, the harm is a side effect. The distinction has nothing to do with how many people die.

lead.text: Apply the test from the last screen to both cases: would the plan still work if the one person were not there?
Now do the sum a utilitarian would do for the footbridge, setting the distinction between means and side effect aside.

reveal.text: The count matches the switch: four more people survive. A theory that only counts outcomes cannot tell the two cases apart.

lead.text: Kant would not be surprised that the count fails to settle the matter. For him, morality starts from what we owe to persons, who can set goals of their own and decide how to live. He called that ability humanity, using the word in his own sense: the rational nature that every person shares.

One of his tests follows from it. Always treat persons as ends in themselves, and never merely as a means. To treat someone as an end is to respect that they have purposes of their own, so you cannot simply override them. Using a person as a tool, as a working part of your plan and without their agreement, fails to show that respect. Kant called this the formula of humanity.

The word 'merely' matters. Using people as means is part of ordinary life, as when you use the baker to get your bread. What the formula forbids is treating someone only as a means, as though their own purposes counted for nothing. The stranger on the footbridge has not agreed to be a brake for the trolley.

steps.headline: Apply the idea of a means to the footbridge push.

workedSteps.text: State the plan: the stranger's body will stop the trolley.
Ask whether the plan works without him. It fails, so his death is how it works.
A plan that needs a person's body treats him as a tool. That is what the formula of humanity forbids.

steps.headline: Name Kant's formulation about how to treat persons.

workedSteps.text: Kant says to treat people always as ends, and never merely as a means.
This is called the formula of ___.

lead.text: Kant gave a second test, and it looks at the rule behind an act and not at who is affected. A maxim is the rule you are acting on, put as 'in this situation I will do this, for this reason'. The test asks whether you could will that everyone act on your maxim. If the maxim only works because most other people do not follow it, you cannot consistently will it for everyone.

Take the maxim of someone who needs money: 'I will promise to repay a loan, knowing I cannot, to get the cash.' Suppose everybody acted on it. Then nobody would believe a promise to repay, since everyone would know that promises are made to be broken. But then no one would lend, and the maxim could not be acted on. It defeats itself. Compare 'I will repay what I borrow', which still works when everyone follows it.

afterFigure.text: This test is called the formula of universal law: act only on a maxim that you can at the same time will to become a universal law. The objection to the false promise is not that universal lying would have bad results. It is that the maxim cannot be consistently universalised, because it depends on a practice, promising, that it would destroy.

premises.text: My maxim: when I need money, I will promise to repay it, knowing I cannot.
If everyone acted on this maxim, no one would believe a promise to repay.
If no one believed such promises, the maxim could not be acted on.

conclusion.text: I cannot will the maxim as a universal law, so the false promise is forbidden.

premises.text: My maxim: when I borrow money, I will repay it as promised.
If everyone acted on this maxim, promises to repay would remain credible.

conclusion.text: I can will this maxim as a universal law.

lead.text: A maxim can be tested the same way whatever its subject. Try one about queues.

reveal.text: That is the formula of universal law: could the maxim hold for everyone? Universalised, this one destroys the queue it relies on.

lead.text: Kant noticed that commands differ in how far they depend on what you happen to want. 'If you want to pass the exam, revise' speaks only to people who have that goal. Someone who does not care about the exam can ignore it. Kant called commands of this kind hypothetical imperatives, since they hold only on a condition.

He thought morality does not work that way. 'Do not use people merely as means' does not say 'if you want to be moral'. It binds you whatever you want, and Kant called a command like that a categorical imperative. The formula of humanity and the formula of universal law are two ways of stating the one categorical imperative of morality.

A categorical command has a different standing from prudent advice. It tells you what to do even when doing it costs you something you wanted. That is why Kant treats keeping a promise as a duty and not only as a sensible policy for being trusted.

steps.headline: Foreseeing a harm and intending it

lead.text: Case A and Case B can now be separated more carefully. In Case A the death of the one is a side effect of turning the trolley. In Case B it is the means. Medieval thinkers worked out a rule built on this same difference, and it is traced to Thomas Aquinas, who discussed killing in self-defence. It is called the doctrine of double effect.

The doctrine says that an act with two effects, one good and one bad, may be allowed when the good effect is what you aim at and the bad one is only foreseen. The bad effect must not be your means to the good one, and the good must outweigh the bad. The standard example is a doctor who gives a dying patient enough painkiller to ease her pain, knowing that it may shorten her life. The lever fits the rule. The footbridge does not, since the stranger's death is the means.
The doctrine gives one of the clearest accounts of why the two cases feel different, though not everyone is satisfied with it.
Apply what you have just read about foreseen effects to a new case, away from trolleys.

reveal.text: The doctrine of double effect: a foreseen side effect may be permitted, while harm intended as a means may not.

blocks.text: A runaway trolley is heading for five people on the main track. In Case A, which you met in the last lesson, you pull a lever and the trolley turns onto a side track, where it kills one person instead. Nearly everyone says that you may pull it.

Case B changes the setting. You are standing on a footbridge above the track, next to a heavy stranger. The only way to stop the trolley is to push him off, so that his body blocks it. One person dies and five live, exactly as in Case A. Yet most people feel at once that pushing him is wrong, even people who would pull the lever without a second thought.

Counting lives cannot explain the difference, since the count is the same. Something else about the two cases must matter. In this lesson you find out what it is, using ideas from the German philosopher Immanuel Kant, and you test them on promises and on a rule that medieval thinkers worked out long before him.

lessons.title: Character and the mean

lead.text: The coach's problem has a familiar kind of solution. Pick an amount that is too much and an amount that is too little. Then take the number halfway between them. That number is the arithmetic mean of the two. You find it by adding them and halving the result, and people often call it the midpoint. If 20 laps is too few for a runner and 40 is too many, the arithmetic mean is 30.

Aristotle used a different example, food for an athlete in training. He says that if ten minae of food is too much for a particular person and two minae too little, the trainer will not necessarily order the amount halfway between. A mina is a Greek unit of weight, a little under half a kilogram. Taking the midpoint would be a tidy rule, and it would give the same amount to everyone. The question is whether it works, and the first step is to find the number it produces.
Use the midpoint rule on Aristotle's numbers: ten minae of food is too much, and two minae is too little.

reveal.text: That is the arithmetic midpoint of the two amounts. Whether it is the right amount for a particular person is what Aristotle goes on to ask.

steps.headline: The midpoint is not the answer

lead.text: Aristotle's next remark is the one that matters. A trainer, he says, will not simply order the midpoint for everybody. Milo of Croton, a famous wrestler, was said to eat enormous meals, and the midpoint would be too little for a man of his size and training. For someone who has just started training, the same amount would be too much.

So the right amount does not sit at one fixed place on the scale. Each person has a range of amounts that suit them. For a champion the range lies above the midpoint, and for a beginner it lies below it. Aristotle called the right amount the mean relative to us, meaning that it depends on who we are and what we face, and cannot be read off the scale alone.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows the scale from two to ten minae with each person's range marked. The arithmetic mean is the same for both, and the two ranges sit in different places. Good judgement follows the person, and a sum cannot do that.

lead.text: Aristotle applied the same thinking to character. A virtue is a lasting good trait of character, and each one concerns a particular area of feeling or action, which he called its sphere. Courage concerns fear and confidence. Too little confidence is the fault of cowardice, and too much is rashness. Courage lies between them.

The faults are called vices. The one with too little is a vice of deficiency and the one with too much is a vice of excess. The virtue is the mean between them: feeling the right amount, at the right time, towards the right things.

afterFigure.text: As with food, the right amount is relative to the person. The picture shows courage for a trained firefighter and for an untrained passer-by. Each is brave when acting within their own range. The firefighter's range sits higher on the scale, because training lets the firefighter rightly face more than an untrained person can.

steps.headline: Place courage for a trained firefighter and for an untrained passer-by.

workedSteps.text: Sphere: fear and confidence. Cowardice has too little confidence and rashness has too much.
The firefighter's right band sits higher on the scale than the passer-by's.
So courage is a mean relative to us, not one fixed point on the scale.

lead.text: The pattern repeats across the virtues. Take anger. Someone who is never angry, even when a friend is mistreated, has a fault of deficiency that Aristotle called lack of spirit. Someone who flares up at every small slight has the fault of excess, irascibility. The virtue between them is good temper: being angry at the right things, with the right people, to the right degree.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows the same sphere in two situations. A stranger who jostles you in a queue calls for very little anger. A parent whose child is in danger can rightly feel a great deal more. The virtue and the scale are the same, and the ranges differ.

Finding the two faults is a useful way to locate a virtue. Name the sphere, ask what going too far looks like and what falling short looks like, and the virtue is what remains between them. The next screen asks you to try this on generosity.

steps.headline: Place generosity between its two vices.

workedSteps.text: Sphere: giving and taking money.
Excess: prodigality, giving too much.
Name the vice of deficiency, giving too little.

lead.text: If the mean differs from person to person, how does anyone come to have a virtue? Aristotle separated two kinds of excellence. Virtues of thought, such as understanding, come mostly from teaching, which takes time and experience. Virtues of character, such as courage, come from habit. He compared character to a craft: we become builders by building and lyre players by playing the lyre, and in the same way we become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave ones.

That is why a passer-by's range and a firefighter's differ. Practice reshapes what each person can rightly face. A beginner who often meets small fears bravely finds the range widening, while one who always runs from fear grows more timid.

afterFigure.text: In the picture, training has moved the band along the scale. Done often enough, an act stops being an effort and becomes a settled part of who you are. Aristotle called the process of forming character by repeated action habituation.

lead.text: Think of how Aristotle says we learn to build or to play the lyre, and apply it to character.

If the mean cannot be read off a scale, something has to find it in each case. Aristotle called that capacity practical wisdom, in Greek phronesis: the ability to see what a situation calls for and to act on it. It cannot be turned into a formula. It grows with experience, as a skilled trainer's sense of how much food a particular wrestler needs grows with years of watching bodies.

The point of having practical wisdom and the virtues is a good life. Aristotle's word for it is eudaimonia, often translated as happiness or flourishing. It does not mean a passing feeling of pleasure. It means living well, which he defined as activity of the soul in accordance with virtue. Virtue is part of what makes a life go well, and does not arrive as a reward afterwards.
Back at the trainer's table, one thing is left to do. The mean relative to us can be measured against the midpoint, and the next question does that.
Go back to the scale of two to ten minae and the arithmetic mean you found at the start. Measure where the beginner's range sits against it.

reveal.text: The beginner's range lies below the midpoint of the scale, so for a beginner the mean relative to us sits below the arithmetic mean.

blocks.text: A coach sets a drill of 20 laps. For a beginner who has only just started running, that is far too much and likely to end in injury. For a champion in training it is hardly a warm-up. The same drill is both too much and too little, and nobody thinks the coach has made a mistake. The mistake would be to hand every runner the same number.

Aristotle, who taught in Athens in the fourth century BCE, thought that character works the same way. Courage and generosity are matters of degree, and each lies somewhere between a fault of too little and a fault of too much. Where it lies depends on the person and the situation. A soldier, a bystander and a parent protecting a child may each need a different amount of nerve.

In this lesson you start with a simple way of finding the middle, see why Aristotle rejected it, and follow his account from food to courage to generosity. You finish with how people come to have these traits at all, and what the traits are for.

lessons.title: The social contract

lead.text: To see what a government is for, imagine living without one. There are no police, no courts, and no one with the power to make rules and enforce them. Philosophers call this the state of nature. It is a thought experiment and not a claim about history. The point is to ask what people would be like, and what they would need, if nothing but themselves stood between them and one another.

Thomas Hobbes, writing during the English Civil War, pictured it darkly. People are roughly equal in strength, in the sense that even the weakest can kill the strongest by cunning or by teaming up with others. Each wants to stay safe, so each fears the rest and may strike first. Competition, fear and pride push everyone towards what Hobbes called a war of all against all.

afterFigure.text: That picture explains his answer to the question of obedience. If the alternative is endless war, any sensible person would give up the freedom to harm others and obey a single ruler, called a sovereign, who is strong enough to keep the peace. Each person makes that deal because every other person does. The agreement is the social contract, and Hobbes thought the sovereign's power should be nearly complete, because only complete power could end the war.

premises.text: Without a common power, each person may do whatever preserves himself.
Even the weakest can kill the strongest, by plot or alliance.
Competition, fear and pride make conflict likely.

conclusion.text: Without a sovereign, life is a war of all against all.

premises.text: In the state of nature a law of nature already forbids harming others.
People leave it only to secure their lives, liberties and property.

conclusion.text: Government is legitimate only by consent, and only within those limits.

lead.text: The picture you have just read ends in a famous line about how bad life without a government would be.

reveal.text: That is Thomas Hobbes, in Leviathan (1651), describing life without a common power.

lead.text: John Locke, writing a generation later, drew a very different picture. In his state of nature people are not at war. They live under a law of nature, a moral law that binds everyone and forbids harming another person's life, liberty or property. The trouble is that nobody is in charge of applying it. People judge their own quarrels, and people favour themselves.

So Locke's people agree to form a government, but their reason is milder than Hobbes's. They want a neutral judge to protect rights they already have. Because they set the government up, its power rests on their consent, their agreement to be governed. Consent also limits it. A government that threatens the lives, liberty and property it was formed to protect has gone beyond the agreement, and the people may replace it.

afterFigure.text: The two pictures agree that government comes from an agreement. They disagree about why people make it and about how far a ruler's power may reach.

steps.headline: Choosing rules without knowing your place

lead.text: The contract tradition returned in the twentieth century with a new question: what would the basic rules of a fair society be? John Rawls proposed a test. Imagine that you must choose the rules for your society before you know where you will stand in it. You do not know whether you will be rich or poor, or what talents you will have. Rawls called the screen that hides all this the veil of ignorance.

A familiar case shows why it helps. When one child cuts a cake and another chooses a slice first, the cutter has every reason to cut evenly, because the cutter does not know which slice will be left. The veil works the same way on a whole society. A rule that favours the rich only looks attractive to someone who knows they are rich, and the veil takes that knowledge away.
Behind the veil you would pick an arrangement that you could live with in whatever place you ended up. The next question tries that on a small scale.
Try the veil with sweets. You choose how to split them, but you do not choose which pile you receive.

reveal.text: Equal piles make the smallest pile as large as it can be. Choosing as if you might be anyone leans towards fairness.

lead.text: Rawls and his critics disagreed about how a person behind the veil should choose. To see the choice, picture a society as three equal groups: a lowest third, a middle third and a top third. A society is described by the income each third receives. You will land in one of the groups, and you do not know which.

One rule is to go by the average. If you are equally likely to land in any group, your expected income is the three incomes added and divided by three, and you choose the society where that is highest. It is the same weighing as in the lesson on consequences. The other rule is maximin, short for maximum minimum: look at the worst position in each society and choose the society whose worst position is best. Rawls argued that when you cannot say how likely each position is, maximin is the prudent rule.

afterFigure.text: In the picture, both societies average 30, so the average rule cannot separate them. The worst-off group gets 20 in P and 12 in Q, so maximin chooses P.

lead.text: Society A pays its three equal groups different incomes. Work out the income you can expect behind the veil.

reveal.text: You averaged the three incomes. Society B's average comes to 30, so on averages alone A looks better.

steps.headline: Compare society A (10, 40, 70) with society C (20, 45, 95) by the average and by maximin.

workedSteps.text: Averages: A is 120 ÷ 3 = 40. C is 160 ÷ 3, about 53.
Worst positions: A pays its lowest group 10 and C pays 20.
C wins on both rules, so there is no dilemma between them here.

lead.text: Maximin looks only at each society's worst position. Compare the lowest income in each society.

reveal.text: B's worst-off group gets 25 and A's gets 10, so maximin picks B even though A has the higher average.

steps.headline: Unequal groups and the difference principle

lead.text: Real societies do not split into equal thirds. Suppose a quarter of the people are in one position and three quarters in another. The average then has to give each income its share of the people: multiply each income by the fraction of people who receive it, and add. The result is a weighted average.

In the picture, Society X pays 20 to the first quarter and 60 to the other three quarters, so its average is 0.25 × 20 + 0.75 × 60 = 50. Society Y pays 28 and 44, which averages 40. On the average rule X wins. Maximin prefers Y, because its worst-off group gets 28 against 20.

afterFigure.text: Maximin ignores the shares. It would choose Y even if the worst-off group were a tiny fraction of the people, and this is the strongest objection to it. John Harsanyi and others argued that a rational chooser should maximise expected utility, which is the average. Rawls turned his side into a rule for real institutions, the difference principle: social and economic inequalities are allowed only if they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged.

lead.text: Real groups differ in size. In Society D a quarter of the people are in one position and three quarters in another.

reveal.text: Maximin ignores the shares and looks only at the worst position, which is the strongest objection to it.

blocks.text: Think about the rules you followed today without being asked. You stopped at a red light and paid for what you bought. Behind all of them stands a government that can punish you if you do not. Most of us accept that arrangement so completely that we rarely ask why we should.

Some philosophers asked it seriously. If nobody has a natural right to rule you, what could give a government that right? Their answer was an agreement made among free people who see that life is better under rules. Different thinkers pictured the agreement differently, and their pictures led to very different governments.

This lesson begins with life before any government and with two of those pictures. It then turns to a thought experiment about a society's basic rules, which asks you to choose them without knowing where in the society you would end up. You test two ways of choosing with numbers, and find that they can point in different directions.

recap.keyIdea: Contract theories ask what people would agree to. Behind the veil, averages and maximin can choose differently.

blocks.text: You averaged incomes for three societies and found where the average and the worst case agree and where they part. You also saw how Hobbes and Locke answer the question of why we obey.
